title: Kulaichev's Sri Yantra is unique
abstract: Nine isosceles triangles with a common axis in a circle of diameter 1 that meet Huet's conditions in Chiodo's form (the two great triangles inscribed, seven apexes on bases, the 18 marmas and the 6 corner touches), Kulaichev's four conditions (a)-(d) and the admissibility of DICTO's paper #103 (Theorem 1) form exactly one figure (identified with the yantra of #103 Theorem 10 through the slope interval). Its slope w7/b7 is proved to lie in an interval of width 2^-21, [0.7504382776..., 0.7504387544...]; #103 gives the slope as 0.7504385160222140244..., a value computed outside Lean that lies in this interval. This settles Kulaichev's 1984 uniqueness question for admissible (well-formed) figures. The proof combines a kernel-checked branch-and-bound interval certificate (64,613 boxes in 10 charts, with proved monotone-split and slope enclosures), a Krawczyk box (uniqueness by a contraction, existence by Banach's fixed-point theorem), the forced construction from the geometry, and a verified sparse-polynomial normaliser for the identities between them. Not formalised: DICTO's study (outside Lean) finds one other real solution of the same equations, at w7/b7 = 0.66866..., which is not admissible (bases out of order, two negative half-widths), so it is not a yantra. Audiences: the history of mathematics (Kulaichev's question in the Indian Journal of History of Science, called still open in 2021), sacred geometry (the construction of the Sri Yantra), and computer-assisted proof in geometry (a certified interval computation checked by Lean's kernel).
